title: Do I need timesheets for R&D tax credits?
description: Timesheets are not required by name to claim the federal R&D tax credit under IRC § 41.
summary: Timesheets are not required by name to claim the federal R&D tax credit under IRC § 41. U.S. taxpayers must keep records sufficient to substantiate wage QREs and allocate employee time to qualified services. Contemporaneous project-level timesheets are the strongest evidence, but corroborated estimates can survive IRS audit when technical documentation proves qualified research occurred.

body.text: Timesheets are not required by name to claim the federal R&D tax credit under IRC § 41. U.S. taxpayers must keep records sufficient to substantiate wage QREs and allocate employee time to qualified services. Contemporaneous project-level timesheets are the strongest evidence, but corroborated estimates can survive IRS audit when technical documentation proves qualified research occurred.
Executive Summary and Statutory Baseline

No provision of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) or the Treasury Regulations requires timesheets by name to claim the federal research and development (R&D) tax credit under IRC § 41. Instead, the governing legal framework operates on an evidentiary sufficiency standard rather than a rigid formatting mandate. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d), a taxpayer claiming a credit under IRC § 41 must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit, operating in tandem with the general tax recordkeeping mandates of IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1. Simultaneously, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1) establishes that whenever an employee performs both qualified and nonqualified services during a taxable year, the taxpayer must allocate wages between those activities—based on the ratio of the employee's time spent performing qualified services to total working time, absent another allocation method that the taxpayer can establish as more appropriate.

Contemporaneous time records—such as project-level timesheets tied directly to discrete business components and experimental activities—represent the most direct mechanism to satisfy both regulatory requirements simultaneously. However, the absence of formal timesheets does not automatically bar a taxpayer from claiming or defending wage qualified research expenses (QREs). When contemporaneous time-tracking systems do not exist, a research credit claim can still survive Internal Revenue Service (IRS) examination and judicial scrutiny, provided the taxpayer satisfies a strict two-step evidentiary burden. First, the taxpayer must establish through credible, predominantly contemporaneous technical documentation that qualified research activities satisfying the statutory four-part test of IRC § 41(d) actually occurred. Second, the taxpayer must anchor employee time estimates in corroborating documentary evidence and testimony from personnel with firsthand operational knowledge of the work performed. Federal appellate courts and the United States Tax Court have accepted reconstructed wage allocations where those prerequisites were met, while consistently disallowing claims that relied on uncorroborated oral testimony, department-wide percentage guesses, or post-hoc credit studies detached from project-level records.
Statutory and Regulatory Requirements for Wage QREs
Recordkeeping Mandates Under Treasury Regulations and IRS Audit Guidelines

The legal architecture governing research credit substantiation deliberately avoids prescribing a uniform accounting or timekeeping artifact across all industries. Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) stipulates that a taxpayer claiming the section 41 credit "must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate" the claimed expenditures, cross-referencing the foundational permanent book-and-record retention obligations of Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1. Recognizing that research documentation varies significantly between software engineering, pharmaceutical development, and heavy manufacturing, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) also authorizes the IRS and taxpayers to enter into collaborative agreements establishing specific recordkeeping guidelines tailored to a taxpayer's operations. Consequently, the regulatory threshold turns on the probative quality, granularity, and verifiability of the underlying evidence rather than whether that evidence takes the form of a daily timesheet.

At the administrative examination level, the IRS Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG, LMSB-04-0508-030, issued May 2008) translates this regulatory standard into operational audit procedures. The RCCATG reiterates that taxpayers must maintain records capable of accurately delineating the specific dollar amounts spent on qualified research activities and emphasizes that information presented to prove or support a research credit claim "should be contemporaneous and available for inspection". This administrative posture creates a structural tension during audits: while Treasury Regulations permit flexible evidentiary formats, IRS examiners trained under the RCCATG evaluate non-contemporaneous reconstructions with heightened skepticism because post-hoc allocations increase the risk of overstating time devoted to resolving technological uncertainties.
Qualifying Wage Expenditures and the Allocation of Services

Time substantiation is central to federal R&D tax credit compliance because employee compensation typically constitutes the largest share of a claimant's total QREs. Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and § 41(b)(2)(D), eligible in-house wage QREs are strictly limited to "wages" as defined in IRC § 3401(a) (federal income tax withholding wages) paid or incurred for "qualified services" performed by an employee. Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B), qualified services are restricted to three statutory categories: engaging in qualified research, engaging in the direct supervision of qualified research, or engaging in the direct support of research activities that constitute qualified research.

Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c) substantially narrows the scope of these three categories, establishing strict boundaries that determine whose time can be included in the credit calculation. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(1), the term "engaging in qualified research" encompasses the actual, hands-on conduct of qualified research, such as an engineer designing and testing an experimental prototype or a scientist conducting laboratory trials. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2), "direct supervision" encompasses exclusively immediate, first-line supervision (management) of qualified research; the regulation explicitly excludes supervision performed by a higher-level manager to whom first-line research managers report, even if that higher-level executive possesses advanced technical credentials or is a qualified research scientist. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(3), "direct support" encompasses services that directly support individuals either engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research or directly supervising those individuals, while excluding general and administrative (G&A) services—such as payroll processing, financial accounting, human resources, or janitorial maintenance—even when performed for or within a dedicated research department.

Because technical personnel, first-line engineering managers, and support technicians almost universally divide their workdays between qualifying experimental tasks and nonqualifying routine activities (such as commercial production support, customer maintenance, or administrative reporting), the wage allocation mandate of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1) becomes the decisive nexus where time records govern audit outcomes. Unless an employee meets the "substantially all" threshold of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2)—whereby at least 80% of an employee's total services during the taxable year consist of qualified services, allowing 100% of their § 3401(a) wages to qualify—the taxpayer must establish the exact fractional share of the employee's total working time devoted to qualified services. A reliable time record or substantiated time allocation provides the examiner with the mathematical numerator and denominator required to verify what proportion of an employee's compensation is legally attributable to qualified services.
The Four-Part Statutory Test Under IRC § 41(d) and the IRC § 174A Amendment

Recording or estimating employee hours is legally meaningless in isolation; time documentation possesses probative value for IRC § 41 purposes only to the extent that the tracked hours map directly to activities satisfying the four-part statutory test of IRC § 41(d). First, under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), the research must be undertaken with respect to expenditures that may be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A. Crucially, practitioners and taxpayers must account for a major statutory revision enacted on July 4, 2025: Public Law 119-21 amended IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) so that the provision now explicitly cross-references expenditures treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A, replacing the prior statutory reference to specified research or experimental expenditures under section 174.

Second, under the technological-in-nature requirement of IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), the activities must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, relying on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, under the business-component requirement of IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), the application of that discovered technological information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer, defined under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business. Fourth, under the process-of-experimentation requirement of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), substantially all of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation relating to a qualified purpose under IRC § 41(d)(3)—specifically, a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality.

Furthermore, any time logged or estimated must exclude activities barred under IRC § 41(d)(4), such as post-commercial-production activities, routine data collection, market research, efficiency surveys, or routine quality control testing. Consequently, a timesheet system that merely tracks attendance or assigns hours to broad department cost centers without linking those hours to specific business components and processes of experimentation fails to substantiate the underlying four-part test.
Why the IRS Prefers Contemporaneous Time Records

Administrative guidance and judicial precedent consistently demonstrate that records created after the close of a tax year carry significantly less evidentiary weight than documentation generated contemporaneously during the execution of the research. This preference stems from the inherent vulnerability of human memory to hindsight bias and financial self-interest when reconstructing technical workflows years after the fact. The RCCATG explicitly instructs revenue agents that the IRS is under no legal obligation to accept taxpayer estimates or extrapolations, linking this administrative authority directly to the taxpayer's statutory recordkeeping duty under IRC § 6001 and stating unequivocally that "arbitrary and unsupported allocations should not be accepted".

In particular, the RCCATG singles out for heightened skepticism claims in which a single flat percentage is selected and applied across total department wage costs—a practice frequently resting on a manager's retrospective recollection—and notes that such allocation percentages may be accepted only when rigorous corroborating prerequisites are satisfied. Judicial authority reinforces this administrative stance: in United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. 2009), the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit held that while a trial court should apply the judicial estimation doctrine once the taxpayer proves that some qualified research activities occurred, the court is not required to accept self-serving estimates prepared years after the tax periods in question.

Tax consultancy literature also frequently characterizes "reasonable basis" as the IRS's substantive legal test for accepting labor time estimates. A rigorous reading of the RCCATG reveals a critical statutory distinction: in the audit guide, the phrase "reasonable basis" appears in the context of the IRC § 6676 penalty on excessive claims for refund or credit, which imposes a 20% penalty on the excessive portion of a claim unless the taxpayer demonstrates that the claim had a reasonable basis. While grounding a wage estimate in a reasonable factual basis is essential for audit defense and penalty avoidance under IRC § 6676, "reasonable basis" is a penalty-exception threshold rather than a formal regulatory substantiation standard under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1) or § 1.41-4(d).
Claiming the Research Credit Without Timesheets
The Cohan Rule and Judicial Limits on Estimation

When a taxpayer lacks contemporaneous timesheets, the legal viability of a research credit claim rests on the judicial doctrine established in Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930). Under the Cohan rule, if a taxpayer demonstrates entitlement to a tax deduction or credit by proving that qualifying activities and expenditures actually occurred, a court may estimate the allowable amount even when the taxpayer cannot produce exact contemporaneous records of the precise figure—though the court may bear heavily against the taxpayer whose inexactitude is of its own making.

In practice, taxpayers invoking Cohan seek to substantiate labor allocations through what a July 2016 article in The Tax Adviser by Jones, Rogers, and Smyth described as an "assortment of documents, interviews, and other evidence" (a formulation occasionally misattributed in commercial R&D credit literature to the IRS or the judiciary itself). However, that same professional analysis underscores that estimates should be avoided wherever possible and relied upon only when supported by unmistakable evidence that qualified research occurred.

Over the past three decades, federal courts have progressively tightened the threshold requirements for invoking Cohan in IRC § 41 disputes. Modern jurisprudence establishes a strict sequential gatekeeping rule: Cohan cannot be used to establish that an activity was qualified research in the first place, nor can it be used when the taxpayer fails to link estimated hours to specific business components. Only after the taxpayer crosses the threshold of proving that qualified services were performed on a qualifying business component can a court use corroborating evidence to estimate the quantity of time spent.
Judicial Precedents Governing Missing or Weak Time Records

The trajectory of federal case law—synthesized through analyses in The Tax Adviser (July 2016 and March 2024) and Current Federal Tax Developments (February 2026)—illustrates the exact evidentiary conditions under which courts accept or reject wage estimates in the absence of timesheets.

cells: Fudim v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1994-235
No formal time-tracking system existed; the company owners estimated that they spent at least 80% of their working time performing qualified services.

The Tax Court applied the Cohan rule and accepted the owners' allocations, which were heavily corroborated by employee testimony, contemporaneous published articles, patents, and the owners' specialized technical backgrounds. However, claimed research time for the owners' daughter was disallowed due to a lack of contemporaneous support.
United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. 2009)
The taxpayer maintained no contemporaneous records tracking the hours worked on research by individual employees.

The Fifth Circuit reversed the district court's categorical refusal to estimate QREs, holding that the Cohan rule should be applied once the evidence establishes that some qualified research activities took place, while noting that courts need not accept estimates prepared long after the credit years.
Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50
The taxpayer lacked exact time tracking for specific production-plant research initiatives and required estimates for qualifying projects.
The Tax Court applied the Cohan rule to estimate allowable wage QREs specifically for the projects that were proven to satisfy the statutory research criteria.
Shami v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2012-78
High-level executive time allocations were claimed without timesheets, resting on oral testimony and general laboratory records.

The Tax Court rejected the estimates in full; the witness testimony was found to be self-serving, contradictory, and uncorroborated, leaving the court with no reasonable factual basis upon which to construct an estimate.
Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201
Wage allocations were based on retrospective percentage estimates prepared by a senior vice president possessing deep institutional knowledge.

The Tax Court accepted the estimates, finding them supported by credible witness testimony and contemporaneous project documents, and noting that the estimates focused on each employee's actual technical activities rather than generic job titles.
Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, aff'd 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023)
Wage estimates were not tied to specific projects or subcomponents and rested primarily on generalized oral testimony.

The claim failed completely; the Seventh Circuit affirmed that time estimates may be utilized only after the taxpayer first establishes with credible evidence that qualified research activities occurred under the "substantially all" experimentation test.
Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20
An executive's claimed research allocation lacked estimates separating qualified research from broader commercial product development activities.
A substantial portion of the executive's wages was disallowed because the record failed to show that the executive acted as a first-line supervisor or provided direct support to qualified research.
Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84
The taxpayers relied on trial testimony without contemporaneous technical documentation tying employee work to qualifying experimentation on specific projects.
The Tax Court declined to apply the Cohan rule, holding that estimation is unavailable without a threshold evidentiary showing that qualified services were actually performed.
George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10
A post-hoc R&D tax credit study claimed wage QREs across multiple projects, only some of which had contemporaneous documentary support.

The Tax Court bifurcated the outcome: credits were allowed for projects where contemporaneous records corroborated the experiments, but denied where contemporaneous records were absent; additionally, Cohan was rejected for base-period expenses where no evidence permitted an informed estimate.

body.text: A deeper examination of this case law reveals a decisive causal pattern across three decades of litigation. In the earlier generation of disputes—exemplified by Fudim (1994), McFerrin (2009), Union Carbide (2009), and Suder (2014)—taxpayers who prevailed without timesheets succeeded because their technical records (patents, engineering schematics, version-control logs, and laboratory notebooks) unequivocally proved that novel experimentation occurred, allowing credible institutional witnesses to bridge the quantitative gap regarding how much time specific individuals devoted to those proven experiments. Even within Fudim, however, the Tax Court demonstrated selective rigor by stripping out the daughter's claimed hours where contemporaneous corroboration was lacking.

Conversely, the modern wave of decisions—spanning Shami (2012), Little Sandy Coal (2021/2023), Moore (2023), Betz (2023), and George (2026)—reflects judicial pushback against commercially packaged R&D credit studies that attempt to substitute retrospective interviews for primary technical evidence. As Little Sandy Coal and Betz establish, taxpayers cannot use oral estimates to bootstrap both the existence of qualified research and the quantification of hours. Furthermore, George v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2026-10) demonstrates two critical audit realities: first, that a post-hoc credit study carries zero independent evidentiary weight unless backed by underlying contemporaneous project records; and second, that lacking historical records for base-period QREs under IRC § 41(c) can defeat a claim just as fatally as lacking credit-year records, because the court will not invoke Cohan to guess base-period expenditures when the record contains no factual foundation for an informed calculation.
Subcomponent Substantiation and the Scope of Eustace v. Commissioner

In industry commentary, Eustace v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2001-66, aff'd 312 F.3d 905 (7th Cir. 2002), is frequently cited for the sweeping proposition that logging employee time in large, undifferentiated blocks labeled simply "R&D" will result in the automatic disallowance of a taxpayer's entire research credit claim. A review of the Tax Court opinion and the Seventh Circuit affirmance reveals a narrower, more precise legal holding.

In Eustace, the taxpayers conceded during litigation that they lacked the documentary substantiation necessary to tie employee salaries to specific research activities at the subcomponent level. Rather than presenting project-level or subcomponent-level records, the taxpayers asked the Tax Court to step in and construct a reasonable allocation of salaries to qualifying software functionality under the Cohan rule. The Tax Court held that Cohan did not compel the court to manufacture an allocation where the taxpayers themselves provided no evidentiary nexus linking employee wages to qualifying subcomponents, and the Seventh Circuit affirmed. The IRS RCCATG specifically cites Eustace to illustrate that courts will deny taxpayers the ability to apply Cohan when claimants fail to substantiate the nexus between salaries and qualifying activities. For compliance design, the operational lesson of Eustace is that time records—whether contemporaneous timesheets or reconstructed allocations—must trace employee effort to the specific business components or subcomponents undergoing experimentation under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) (the shrinking-back rule), rather than aggregating hours into a generic, company-wide "R&D" cost bucket.
Corroborating Evidence Supporting a Time Estimate
IRS Audit Techniques Guide Standards for Wage QRE Examination

When formal timesheets are unavailable or incomplete, taxpayers must construct an evidentiary mosaic that satisfies the examination criteria set forth in the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 - Qualified Research Expenses (issued June 2005). The June 2005 QRE ATG states that the fundamental objective of an examiner reviewing in-house wage QREs is twofold: determining what the employee actually did during the tax year, and determining how much time the employee spent doing it.

To answer those two questions in the absence of dedicated project timesheets, the June 2005 IRS ATG explicitly identifies several categories of existing business records as reliable sources of substantiating information, specifically naming payroll records that establish base compensation and employment periods, employee job descriptions detailing assigned technical responsibilities, annual or periodic performance evaluations documenting completed milestones and project assignments, and employee calendars and appointment books reflecting day-to-day project meetings, testing schedules, and development cycles. In addition to documentary records, the June 2005 QRE ATG instructs examiners that oral interviews should be considered to supplement and corroborate information derived from existing contemporaneous documents. However, the May 2008 RCCATG adds a vital qualification regarding witness credibility: examiners are directed to verify whether oral testimony and interview responses come directly from the employees who actually performed the research, rather than solely from third-party consultants or high-level executives removed from day-to-day experimentation.
Evidentiary Hierarchy and Source-Specific Substantiation Frameworks

While this four-tier grouping represents a practitioner compliance framework rather than an official IRS classification, mapping its elements against primary IRS audit guides and Tax Court precedent clarifies which specific documents carry authoritative weight during an examination.

headers: Regulatory, IRS ATG, and Judicial Verification Status

cells: Foundational Financial Records
Form W-2 wage statements, payroll registers, and corporate organizational charts.
Partially Listed in IRS ATG: Payroll records are explicitly recognized in the June 2005 IRS QRE ATG.
Secondary Time Indicators
Employee job descriptions, performance evaluations, calendars, appointment books, time questionnaires, and email logs.

Bifurcated Status: Job descriptions, performance evaluations, calendars, and appointment books are explicitly verified as recommended sources in the June 2005 IRS QRE ATG. Conversely, "time questionnaires" and "email logs" come from practitioner methodologies and do not appear in the IRS ATG.
Technical Corroboration
Design specifications, test plans, experimental results, engineering meeting minutes, and process flowcharts.

Judicially Validated: While framed as consultancy examples, Tax Court jurisprudence—including Fudim, Suder, Betz, and George—confirms that contemporaneous technical records carry decisive evidentiary weight in proving that qualified experimentation occurred. However, consultancy phrases claiming that secondary records provide "contemporaneity in spirit" have no basis in IRS guidance.
Attestation and Estimate
Structured subject-matter expert interviews and formal management attestations.

Corroborative Supplement Only: The June 2005 IRS ATG endorses interviews strictly to supplement and corroborate existing documentary records. Under the May 2008 RCCATG and Little Sandy Coal, interviews and attestations cannot substitute for missing technical documentation and carry weight primarily when provided by personnel who personally performed the research.

body.text: A critical legal pitfall arises within the "Attestation and Estimate" tier when taxpayers rely on interviews with senior executives or department heads. Some practitioner materials describe interviewing "higher-level research managers" whose own wages were also allocated to qualified services. While interviewing a higher-level manager can legitimately help establish historical facts about a company's research portfolio (as occurred with the senior vice president in Suder v. Commissioner), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2) strictly bars treating supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report as "direct supervision". As reinforced in Moore v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2023-20), a higher-level manager's compensation qualifies for the research credit only to the fractional extent that the executive personally engaged in the hands-on conduct of qualified research or provided direct technical support, requiring separate, rigorous substantiation of those personal hands-on hours.
Structured Estimation Methodologies and Fractional Attribution
Role-Based Time Estimation Frameworks and Fee Structure Incentives

This approach begins by extracting baseline IRC § 3401(a) compensation from payroll registers, cross-referencing employee roles against contemporaneous technical artifacts and secondary time indicators (such as sprint logs, calendars, and performance evaluations), and then conducting structured interviews with technical personnel to assign a specific fractional percentage of each employee's time to qualified services.

Two structural elements of this practitioner model are verifiable in primary firm disclosures. This three-tier stratification aligns closely with the IRS RCCATG's warning against arbitrary, department-wide percentage allocations and the Tax Court's preference in Suder for individualized, activity-focused estimates. From an audit risk perspective, IRS examiners closely scrutinize contingency-fee credit studies precisely because preparer compensation tied to credit size correlates strongly with inflated executive wage allocations and unsupported department-wide percentages.

At the same time, rigorous technical analysis requires filtering out unsubstantiated promotional claims that frequently appear in commercial R&D tax marketing materials. Specifically, promotional figures asserting exact audit defense success rates of 98% for contemporaneous timesheets, 92% for consultancy-prepared role estimates, and 35% for ad hoc guesses—as well as generalized claims that insufficient documentation reduces claim values by 30% to 100% or that timesheets represent an official worldwide "gold standard"—lack any independent empirical source or IRS statistical verification and cannot be relied upon as factual benchmarks.
Quantitative Application of Fractional Attribution

To illustrate how fractional attribution operates under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1) when timesheets are absent, consider an illustrative compliance scenario involving a mid-level mechanical engineer. Suppose the engineer earns $100,000 in IRC § 3401(a) wages during the taxable year, works 2,000 total hours, and does not maintain daily timesheets. During a structured compliance review, engineering calendars, two-week Agile sprint records, and laboratory test reports—corroborated during a recorded technical interview with the engineer—establish that the engineer spent 1,200 of those 2,000 working hours conducting qualifying experiments on a single new business component, with the remaining 800 hours spent on routine commercial manufacturing support and administrative duties.
Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1), the fractional allocation of the engineer's time to qualified services is calculated as follows:
Qualified Service Fraction = (Hours Spent on Qualified Services) / (Total Working Hours) = 1,200 / 2,000 = 0.60 (or 60%)
Applying this substantiated fraction to the engineer's eligible IRC § 3401(a) compensation yields the allowable wage QRE:
Allowable Wage QRE = $100,000 × 0.60 = $60,000

Because the 60% allocation falls below the 80% "substantially all" threshold of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2), only the allocated $60,000 may be included in the IRC § 41 credit calculation. More importantly, under the judicial standards established in Little Sandy Coal, Betz, and Eustace, as well as the administrative directives of the RCCATG, this $60,000 wage QRE will survive IRS examination only if two conditions are demonstrated in the audit file: first, the contemporaneous test reports and sprint records must independently prove that the project satisfied all four elements of IRC § 41(d); and second, the 60% factor must be demonstrably derived from that specific engineer's hours on that specific business component rather than extrapolated from a generic engineering department average.
Statistical and Judgment Sampling for Large Research Credit Claims

For enterprise taxpayers employing hundreds or thousands of engineers and scientists across dozens of business units, reconstructing or auditing individual time allocations for every employee is operationally prohibitive. As noted in the June 2005 IRS QRE ATG, statistical sampling techniques provide a recognized mechanism to evaluate large employee pools. However, taxpayers and practitioners must understand the procedural rules governing how the IRS deploys sampling during an examination, as set forth in the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Sampling Methodologies (June 2005) and the IRS Large Business and International (LB&I) Field Directive on Use of Sampling Methodologies in Research Credit Cases.

Under the IRS Sampling Methodologies ATG, sampling should be considered whenever examining the entire population of research projects or employees would require excessive time or resources. Crucially, sampling in this context is an IRS examination tool designed during the audit: the revenue agent, working in conjunction with an IRS Computer Audit Specialist (CAS), meets with the taxpayer to jointly design the sampling plan and define the sampling unit.

Furthermore, the IRS LB&I Field Directive on sampling in research credit cases—which explicitly notes that it is an internal administrative directive rather than an official pronouncement of law—draws a sharp legal distinction between judgmental sampling and statistical sampling. A judgment sample, in which sample items are selected based on examiner judgment rather than mathematical probability, requires the written consent of the taxpayer to project the results across the population, whereas a valid statistical sample using random or stratified probability selection with measurable precision and confidence intervals does not require taxpayer consent. The IRS Sampling Methodologies ATG frames the requirement for judgment samples as obtaining taxpayer assent to how the sample results will be applied to the broader population, which is generally executed through a formal closing agreement on Form 906 (Closing Agreement on Final Determination Covering Specific Matters). The ATG explicitly warns examiners that without a signed Form 906 closing agreement, population-wide adjustments extrapolated from a judgment sample may not be sustainable in federal court.
Comparative Timesheet Standards Outside the Federal R&D Tax Credit

Taxpayers and compliance officers frequently conflate the flexible substantiation standards of IRC § 41 with far stricter timekeeping regimes mandated under federal defense procurement rules or state labor laws. Distinguishing these external regulatory frameworks prevents organizations from either over-engineering unnecessary tax compliance barriers or misapplying non-tax legal rules to R&D credit audits.
Defense Contract Audit Agency Accounting System Requirements

Organizations performing cost-reimbursement contracts for the U.S. Department of Defense operate under the stringent oversight of the Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA). According to official DCAA presentations on pre-award and post-award accounting system requirements, government contractors must charge direct and indirect labor based strictly on contemporaneous timekeeping documents that are personally completed and certified by the employee and formally approved by a supervisor. Furthermore, DCAA guidelines instruct that employees must record their time daily across all work performed, capturing all hours worked including uncompensated overtime—a practice commonly referred to in government contracting as "total time accounting" (though accounting advisory firm Forvis Mazars notes that the phrase "total time accounting" is not formally defined in the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR)). While some secondary consultancy articles claim that DCAA timekeeping failures automatically result in "negligent fraud findings" or mandate specific software lockouts, those specific characterizations are not confirmed in primary DCAA guidance. More importantly, DCAA daily sign-off rules apply solely to federal procurement cost accounting and do not govern IRC § 41 research credit substantiation.
State Wage-and-Hour Rounding Jurisprudence: Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC

Commercial time-tracking literature occasionally asserts that "recent court decisions mandate minute-by-minute accuracy" for employee timekeeping, including meal and rest breaks. Tracing this claim to primary jurisprudence reveals that it refers to the California Supreme Court's decision in Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC, No. S253677 (Cal. Feb. 25, 2021). In Donohue, the California Supreme Court held that employers subject to California wage-and-hour laws cannot use neutral time-rounding policies (such as rounding punches to the nearest 5, 10, or 15 minutes) when recording employee meal-period punches, because rounding infringes on California's statutory mandate for a full 30-minute meal break. This ruling is strictly a California state labor law rule governing meal-period compliance for non-exempt hourly workers; it does not establish a federal tax rule or require minute-by-minute timesheet precision for exempt salaried engineers claiming the IRC § 41 credit. Similarly, widely circulated vendor blog statistics—such as claims by timekeeping software vendors citing QuickBooks pages that "up to 80% of timesheets require corrections" or that poorly tracked time costs the U.S. economy billions of dollars annually—are unverified commercial marketing statements with no relevance to federal tax law.
General IRS Recordkeeping Guidance Under IRC § 6001

Practitioner articles also occasionally cite the general IRS small-business guidance page titled "What kind of records should I keep" for the proposition that timesheets and payroll registers are required to substantiate labor costs. A direct audit of that official IRS publication confirms that while the page instructs businesses to retain payroll and employment tax records, it makes no mention of timesheets. Across both general IRC § 6001 guidance and specific IRC § 41 regulations, the IRS refrains from mandating timesheets as an exclusive recordkeeping medium.

body.text: Audit Defense Synthesis and Practical Compliance Takeaways

Synthesizing the statutory text of IRC § 41, Treasury Regulations, IRS Audit Techniques Guides, and federal case law through 2026 yields a cohesive compliance framework for organizations evaluating or defending wage QREs. Foremost, timesheets represent an evidentiary best practice rather than a statutory prerequisite: neither IRC § 41 nor Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) mandates timesheets by name, yet contemporaneous project-level time tracking remains the single strongest defense for the fractional wage allocation required under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1), eliminating the need to rely on judicial estimation under the Cohan rule. For taxpayers that do utilize time-tracking software, activity-specific project codes significantly outperform generic "R&D" buckets. Logging hours to a single, undifferentiated "R&D" or "Engineering" cost code creates severe vulnerability under Eustace v. Commissioner and the IRS RCCATG; instead, time-tracking codes should map directly to discrete business components (or subcomponents) and specific phases of experimentation so that nonqualifying routine maintenance, post-production support, and administrative activities are cleanly segregated at the point of entry.

Where formal timesheets do not exist, contemporaneous technical artifacts serve as the indispensable prerequisite for any labor estimate. As demonstrated in Little Sandy Coal, Betz, and George v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2026-10), courts will refuse to apply the Cohan rule to estimate employee hours unless the taxpayer first proves through contemporaneous technical records—such as design specifications, test protocols, commit logs, prototype trial results, and engineering meeting minutes—that qualified research activities under IRC § 41(d) and IRC § 174A actually occurred. Filing and dating technical records as work progresses establishes the factual bedrock required to support any subsequent labor allocation.

Furthermore, individualized corroboration must replace department-wide percentages whenever employee hours are reconstructed. Wage estimates must be constructed individually for each employee based on their specific technical activities (as validated in Suder v. Commissioner), corroborated by secondary time indicators recognized in the June 2005 IRS ATG (job descriptions, performance evaluations, calendars, and appointment books) and direct interviews with the personnel who performed the work. Blanket percentage allocations applied across an entire department's payroll should be strictly avoided, and higher-level managers' wages must be excluded unless those executives personally conducted or directly supported qualified research under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c). Finally, maintaining audit trail integrity strengthens evidentiary credibility: while automated approval workflows and locked timesheet periods stem from DCAA government contracting standards rather than IRS regulations, implementing basic version control and supervisor sign-off on either timesheets or periodic time-allocation surveys demonstrates to IRS examiners that records were generated in the ordinary course of business rather than fabricated or altered retroactively for a tax audit.
